title: 1 Kings 1:1–10
context: King David is old and advanced in years, and though they cover him with clothes he cannot keep warm. His servants propose that a young virgin be sought to stand before the king, cherish him, and lie in his bosom so that he may keep warm. They search the borders of Israel, find Abishag the Shunammite, and bring her to the king. The narrator says that she was very beautiful, that she cherished the king and served him, and then states the limit of the scene: “the king didn’t know her intimately.” The notes should not go beyond that wording. In the same setting Adonijah the son of Haggith exalts himself, saying, “I will be king.” and prepares chariots, horsemen, and fifty men to run before him. His father had not displeased him at any time by asking why he had done so; he was very handsome, and he was born after Absalom. He confers with Joab the son of Zeruiah and with Abiathar the priest, and they help him. Zadok the priest, Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, Nathan the prophet, Shimei, Rei, and the mighty men who belonged to David are not with him. Adonijah kills sheep, cattle, and fatlings by the stone of Zoheleth, beside En Rogel, and invites his brothers and the men of Judah, the king’s servants, but he does not call Nathan, Benaiah, the mighty men, or Solomon his brother. Both traditions read the unit as the weakness of David’s last days set beside Adonijah’s self-exaltation, and they treat Abishag only as the narrator describes her.

verses.text: Now King David was old and advanced in years; and they covered him with clothes, but he couldn’t keep warm.
verses.arminianNotes:
The book opens with David already on the throne, “old and advanced in years;” covered with clothes, yet unable to keep warm. The sentence is a simple report of age and weakness, not a symbol layered on the text.

Arminian readers hear a real decline at the end of a long reign. The king’s body fails, and the court must deal with that fact before any question of who will sit after him is raised.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the opening as a dated scene of David’s last days. He is still king, but he cannot keep warm, and the narrative does not hide that frailty.

Both traditions start from that shared ground. The verse sets the condition under which Abishag will be brought and Adonijah will make his move, without turning the king’s age into an allegory.

verses.text: Therefore his servants said to him, “Let a young virgin be sought for my lord the king. Let her stand before the king, and cherish him; and let her lie in your bosom, that my lord the king may keep warm.”
verses.arminianNotes:
David’s servants propose a practical remedy: “Let a young virgin be sought for my lord the king.” She is to stand before him, cherish him, and “lie in your bosom, that my lord the king may keep warm.” The reason they name is warmth, not marriage and not a claim on the throne.

Arminian readers keep the proposal inside those words. The verse should be read soberly, without adding intimacy or motive that the servants do not state.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also refuse to press the language past what the servants say. The young woman is sought so that the king may keep warm, and later verses will tell what did and did not follow.

Both traditions treat the proposal as court care for an aged king. Nothing beyond the text should be read into “lie in your bosom” here.

verses.text: So they sought for a beautiful young lady throughout all the borders of Israel, and found Abishag the Shunammite, and brought her to the king.
verses.arminianNotes:
The search is carried “throughout all the borders of Israel,” and they find “Abishag the Shunammite” and bring her to the king. The narrator gives her name and her place of origin, and he does not pause for a character study.

Arminian readers take the finding as it is told. She is brought because she was sought, and her later appearance in chapter 2 should not be loaded back into this verse.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise leave Abishag as the woman named here, a Shunammite found and brought to the king. Site and family details beyond that name are not supplied.

Both traditions introduce her as the narrative does, without speculation about her future or about the king’s household beyond this scene.

verses.text: The young lady was very beautiful; and she cherished the king, and served him; but the king didn’t know her intimately.
verses.arminianNotes:
The narrator says, “The young lady was very beautiful; and she cherished the king, and served him; but the king didn’t know her intimately.” That last clause is the limit of the report. She cherished and served him; the king did not know her intimately.

Arminian readers stop there. The verse is to be handled soberly. It neither invites nor permits a description of intimacy beyond what it states, and it does not turn Abishag into a symbol.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hold the same limit. Beauty, care, and service are named, and then the narrator closes the door: “the king didn’t know her intimately.”

Both traditions keep the wording and refuse to say more. Later, when Adonijah asks for her, that request must be read in its own place, not by inventing a relationship the text has denied here.

verses.text: Then Adonijah the son of Haggith exalted himself, saying, “I will be king.” Then he prepared him chariots and horsemen, and fifty men to run before him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Then Adonijah the son of Haggith exalted himself, saying, “I will be king.” He prepares chariots, horsemen, and fifty men to run before him. The claim is his own, and it is public in form even if David has not granted it.

Arminian readers hear a real act of self-exaltation. Adonijah does not wait to be named; he declares himself and gathers the signs of a royal procession.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the move is Adonijah’s. “I will be king.” is his word, not a word from David or from the LORD in this verse.

Both traditions describe the bid as the narrator gives it. The chariots and runners may recall earlier display in David’s house, but the verse itself is about Adonijah’s present claim, not a forced type.

verses.text: His father had not displeased him at any time in saying, “Why have you done so?” and he was also a very handsome man; and he was born after Absalom.
verses.arminianNotes:
The narrator adds that David “had not displeased him at any time in saying, “Why have you done so?” Adonijah was “a very handsome man;” and “he was born after Absalom.” The father’s failure to check him, his appearance, and his place among David’s sons are given as facts of the house.

Arminian readers hear a real history of indulgence. David’s silence is not excused or turned into a decree; it is part of how Adonijah came to act as he does.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise let the verse stand as a comment on David’s household. The handsome son born after Absalom has not been asked, “Why have you done so?”

Both traditions take the notice as explanation, not as a party argument about parenting or providence. The text names what David had not done, and it names Adonijah’s place after Absalom, without further claim.

verses.text: He conferred with Joab the son of Zeruiah and with Abiathar the priest; and they followed Adonijah and helped him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Adonijah “conferred with Joab the son of Zeruiah and with Abiathar the priest; and they followed Adonijah and helped him.” The commander and a priest stand with the claimant. Their later fate is not yet told; this verse only records the alliance.

Arminian readers hear a free and costly choice. Joab and Abiathar are not forced into the conference; they confer, follow, and help.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also start from the alliance as a real act. Joab and Abiathar lend their names and their offices to Adonijah’s bid, and the narrative will remember that help.

Both traditions describe the support without turning it into a verdict already executed. The verse records who stood with Adonijah at the start.

verses.text: But Zadok the priest, Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, Nathan the prophet, Shimei, Rei, and the mighty men who belonged to David, were not with Adonijah.
verses.arminianNotes:
A second list follows: “Zadok the priest, Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, Nathan the prophet, Shimei, Rei, and the mighty men who belonged to David, were not with Adonijah.” The priest, the captain, the prophet, and David’s mighty men stand apart, together with Shimei and Rei.

Arminian readers take the list as a real division at court. This Shimei is not identified here with Shimei the son of Gera in the next chapter, and Rei is not otherwise explained; both names should be left as the verse gives them.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise refuse to merge figures the text does not merge. Zadok, Benaiah, Nathan, and the mighty men will appear again in Solomon’s anointing; Shimei and Rei are simply among those who were not with Adonijah.

Both traditions read the verse as the other side of the court, shared ground for the conflict that follows, without invented identifications.

verses.text: Adonijah killed sheep, cattle, and fatlings by the stone of Zoheleth, which is beside En Rogel; and he called all his brothers, the king’s sons, and all the men of Judah, the king’s servants;
verses.arminianNotes:
Adonijah “killed sheep, cattle, and fatlings by the stone of Zoheleth, which is beside En Rogel;” and he called his brothers, the king’s sons, and the men of Judah, the king’s servants. The feast has the form of a sacrifice and a gathering of the royal house, at a place the narrator names and does not map.

Arminian readers take Zoheleth and En Rogel as given place names. Traditional identifications near Jerusalem may be mentioned only as common suggestions, not as settled fact.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also decline to turn the site into a certainty beyond the text. The stone and the spring locate the feast, and the guests are the brothers and the men of Judah.

Both traditions describe a public sacrificial meal in support of Adonijah’s claim, without forcing a typological reading of the place or of the guests.

verses.text: but he didn’t call Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah, and the mighty men, and Solomon his brother.
verses.arminianNotes:
The invitation has a sharp edge: “but he didn’t call Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah, and the mighty men, and Solomon his brother.” Those who were not with him in verse 8 are not called to the feast, and Solomon is named last.

Arminian readers hear a deliberate exclusion. The feast is not a gathering of the whole court; the prophet, the captain, the mighty men, and the brother who will be discussed next are left out.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same omission. Solomon is already on the list of those Adonijah will not have at En Rogel, and Nathan is already outside the circle.

Both traditions close the unit on that shared observation. The bid is under way, and the people who will act in the next passage have not been called.
